title: From Printed Laughter to kkkk: Linguistic Change, Iconicity and Documentary Evidence in the History of Written Laughter in Portuguese
content: This study examines whether historical written laughter in Portuguese can be linked to digital kkkk. An exploratory, non-probability documentary design combines historical linguistics, iconicity and source criticism. Sixteen requested entry points are organized into thirteen operational access-resource groups. The inventories include documents dating back to 1645 and 40 source identifiers predating 1900, without continuous annual coverage of that period. The core contains 121 records: 96 descriptive laughter annotations and 25 mimetic representations or digital markers, including 110 records from 1900 to 2009, one per year, and 11 outside that interval. The core spans 1872–2025. Archive-by-decade selection comprises 135 selection links and 129 source identifiers: 65 links were confirmed in the indicated archive and 70 through alternative sources. Two fixed newspaper items yielded no attestation in visual inspection; literary alternatives for their periods are recorded separately. All 66 initial bibliographic leads were audited, but none of the 22 alleged quotations was fully authenticated. Historical forms and digital kkkk are documented, including a 2008 dissertation reporting research conducted in 2007. These findings establish neither an absolute origin nor a transmission chain from nineteenth-century writing. Sampling and detection calculations are prospective scenarios, not population estimates from this collection. Descriptive analysis and exploratory clustering of 16 normalized graphic sequences selected 4 hierarchical groups and 6 K-means groups within the tested grid; these are not evolutionary stages. Resemblance alone does not demonstrate descent, and documentary gaps do not demonstrate independence. Public data and scripts support review of evidence, counts and limitations.
